title: Metaphysics
content_html:
Metaphysics

Metaphysics is a branch of philosophy that studies the fundamental nature of reality—what exists, what it means for something to exist, and how things relate to each other. The term comes from Aristotle’s writings: the works placed “after the Physics” (Greek: meta ta physika), which explored questions beyond the study of nature.

Traditionally, metaphysics is divided into several core areas:

  • Ontology: the study of being and existence. What kinds of things exist? For example: numbers, minds, time, possibilities—are these real or just concepts?
  • Identity and Change: what makes something the same over time, even as it changes? How can a river or a person remain “the same” through transformation?
  • Space and Time: what are space and time—substances, relations, or constructs of the mind?
  • Causality and Possibility: what does it mean for one thing to cause another? Could the world have been otherwise?
  • Mind and Reality: how does consciousness relate to the physical world? Is mind reducible to matter, or something fundamentally different?

Metaphysics is often contrasted with:

  • Epistemology (the study of knowledge—how we know what we know),
  • Ethics (the study of how we should live),
  • Logic (the study of valid reasoning).

Key Metaphysical Problems

Topic Central Questions Examples
Ontology (Being) What exists? What kinds of things are fundamental? Do numbers exist? Is “nothingness” real?
Identity & Change How can something remain the same despite change? Is a river still the same river as it flows? Ship of Theseus.
Space & Time Are they independent realities or relational? Is time real (eternalism vs. presentism)?
Causation What does it mean for X to cause Y? Does correlation imply causation? Quantum indeterminacy?
Modality What does it mean that something is possible, necessary, or impossible? Could the laws of physics have been otherwise?
Mind & Body Is mind reducible to matter? Dualism vs. physicalism vs. panpsychism.
Universals & Particulars Are properties real (redness, beauty) or just concepts? Does “redness” exist beyond red objects?
Free Will & Determinism Do we truly choose, or is everything determined? Neuroscience vs. moral responsibility.
God & the Absolute Is there a necessary being? What is the ultimate ground of reality? Classical theism vs. atheism vs. process philosophy.

Metaphysics is both ancient and evolving: from Aristotle’s “study of being” → medieval theology → Kant’s critique → modern skepticism → today’s analytic and continental approaches. Its core problems—existence, time, causation, identity, mind—remain central, even when addressed by science.

Models

Physics and metaphysics are models we create to make sense of experience. They don’t show the universe “as it is,” only how it appears to minds like ours. The structures of space, time, and causality are not features of the world-in-itself, but the conditions under which humans can experience a world. Our brains evolved to track regularities in sensory input — not necessarily to mirror reality perfectly, but to predict outcomes useful for survival. If physics and metaphysics are internally coherent frameworks, they may be “self-sufficient” — able to generate explanations, predictions, and meaning without needing to be mirrors of reality. This is like a mathematical system: once axioms are chosen, the rest follows logically, regardless of whether it corresponds to anything “real.”

Despite being mind-constructed, physics works: we can land probes on other planets, build semiconductors, predict eclipses. This pragmatic success suggests at least a correspondence between our models and external regularities — though not necessarily a one-to-one “mirror.” Some philosophers call this structural realism: we don’t know the nature of reality itself, but our models capture its structure well enough for predictions. Physics/metaphysics could be mind-world co-constructions: the brain imposes form (categories, concepts), and the world pushes back (empirical constraint). In this view, science and metaphysics are interfaces: not the thing-in-itself, but adaptive translations. They may not “reflect” the universe in a mirror sense, but they are effective relational maps between mind and world.

Buddhist direct knowledge

A key difference between many strands of Western philosophy and Buddhism is that Buddhism claims that direct knowledge is possible. Through meditative insight (vipassanā), the mind can perceive reality as it truly is, not just filtered through concepts. The three marks of existence: impermanence (anicca), unsatisfactoriness (dukkha), and non-self (anattā) — can be understood not intellectually but directly, experientially. Everything arises in dependence on conditions, and the Buddha taught this as a structure observable through deep contemplation.

Human knowledge is always mediated by categories of the mind (space, time, causality); we cannot access the “thing-in-itself” (noumenon). There are limits to reason. Science can test models against phenomena, but Buddhism claims the observer can see through the phenomena themselves. Buddhism accepts that reason is limited, but consciousness can be trained to go beyond conceptual mediation. Texts describe the Buddha as having “direct knowledge” (abhiññā) of the cosmos, karmic causality, and past lives. Crucially, this is not framed as speculative metaphysics, but as practical insight into the nature of existence that ends suffering.
